title: They readily grant that the power to the contrary stands with the act itself
source_text: XX. Caeterum facile concedent, ab eo quem gratia movet, exempli causa, ad orandum, & eleemosynam pauperi largiendam, non omnino propterea tolli potentiam non orandi, & eleemosynam illam non largiendi; imo cum ipso actu invocandi & dandi eleemosynam non minus stare potentiam ad privationem illorum actuum, aut etiam ad actus contrarios, quam cum actu loquendi stat potestas silendi, & cum actu sedendi stat potestas non sedendi, aut etiam ambulandi.
pass_a_gloss: However they will readily grant, that from him whom grace moves, for example, to praying, and to bestowing alms on a poor man, the power of not praying, and of not bestowing that alms is not at all on that account taken away; nay that with the very act of calling upon God and giving alms the power to the privation of those acts, or also to contrary acts, stands no less, than with the act of speaking stands the power of being silent, and with the act of sitting stands the power of not sitting, or also of walking.
pass_b_english: Still, they will readily admit that when grace moves someone to pray, say, or to give alms to a poor man, his power not to pray and not to give those alms is not removed on that account.

Indeed, the power to leave those acts undone, or even to do the opposite, coexists with the very act of praying and of giving alms just as much as the power to keep silent coexists with the act of speaking, and the power not to sit, or even to walk, coexists with the act of sitting.

lemmas.gloss: to the privation of those acts

choices.why: Kept as the technical phrase both Reformed parties use; it marks the necessity that removes the power to act otherwise, as against a necessity of infallibility.
